title: Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
intro: This domain covers how architects prove that a Claude-based system works, keep it working, and make it faster and cheaper without breaking it. The exam tests judgment more than vocabulary: given a scenario with symptoms, constraints, and partial data, you must choose the right metric, testing method, diagnosis, or optimization — and recognize the tempting option that measures the wrong thing, confounds an experiment, or treats a symptom instead of a cause. Expect questions that hinge on sequencing (measure before optimizing, offline before online) and on matching methods to output types and workload shapes.

objectives.objective: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
objectives.explanation:
Evaluation starts before any code is written: an architect translates the business requirement into measurable pass criteria across five dimensions — accuracy (does the system produce correct, useful output for the task), latency (how fast, measured where users feel it), cost (what each outcome costs to produce), safety (does it avoid harmful or policy-violating output), and security (does it resist manipulation such as prompt injection). Defining these targets up front turns iteration into engineering; defining them after the fact turns evaluation into rationalization.

Each dimension has a right and a wrong way to measure. Accuracy for high-stakes generation usually needs a dedicated faithfulness or grounding metric — a holistic quality score can be high while the output contains fabricated claims. Latency must be reported as percentiles (p95, p99) and time-to-first-token, because averages hide the tail behavior users actually experience. Cost is only meaningful per successful task outcome: a cheap-per-token model that triggers retries and human correction can cost more per completed task than a premium one. Safety and security need leading metrics — harmful-output rate and injection success rate measured against adversarial test suites run on the deployed system — not lagging metrics like incident counts, which only move after users have been harmed.

The leading-versus-lagging distinction runs through the whole domain. Business outcomes like churn and CSAT validate the system over quarters, but they are slow, noisy composites that cannot steer a two-week release cycle. Iteration needs fast, attributable proxies — golden-set pass rate, per-release accuracy — paired with the slow outcomes they are meant to predict. An architect who can name which metric answers which question, at which timescale, has the core skill this objective tests.
objectives.whyItMatters: Every downstream activity — building eval sets, running A/B tests, diagnosing failures, optimizing cost — inherits its meaning from the metrics chosen here. A system optimized against the wrong metric gets confidently worse: teams have shipped assistants with rising quality scores and rising fabrication rates because nobody measured grounding, and met latency SLAs on paper while peak-hour users suffered, because the SLA was written on the mean. In production, metric definition is where evaluation succeeds or fails before it begins.

examples.title: Choosing metrics for a claims-processing assistant
examples.body: An insurer is comparing two designs for automated claims extraction. Design A uses a cheaper model but fails validation more often, triggering retries and adjuster corrections; Design B costs more per token but usually succeeds first pass. Framed as cost per million tokens, A wins. The architect reframes the comparison as cost per successfully completed claim — API spend across all attempts plus adjuster correction time — and B wins decisively. The same discipline applies to the accuracy metric: instead of one overall quality score, the team defines field-level extraction accuracy plus a faithfulness check that every extracted value appears in the source document, because a fabricated policy number is a different and worse failure than a missing one.

examples.title: Writing a latency SLA that reflects users
examples.body: A retailer's chatbot team reports 1.8s average latency against a 3s SLA, yet evening complaints spike. The architect rewrites the SLA in percentiles: p95 under 3s and time-to-first-token under 800ms, measured during peak windows. Instrumentation then shows p99 hitting 14 seconds at peak — fully compatible with the healthy-looking mean. The lesson generalizes: means summarize the experience nobody has, while percentiles describe the worst experiences enough users have to matter, and time-to-first-token captures perceived responsiveness for streamed replies.

pitfalls: Setting quality bars after seeing system performance — this calibrates the target to whatever ships instead of to the business need, and 'we'll know it when we see it' reliably drifts toward acceptance.
Reporting average latency for an SLA — averages hide tail behavior, and the users in the p95-p99 tail are the ones who complain and churn.
Comparing designs on per-token price — tokens are an input cost; the meaningful unit is cost per successful outcome, including retries and human correction.
Using post-launch incident counts as the security metric — incidents are lagging indicators; injection resistance must be measured pre-release with adversarial suites against the deployed system.
Trusting one holistic quality score for high-stakes output — a summary can score 9/10 on 'quality' while containing fabricated dosages; grounding needs its own metric.

objectives.objective: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
objectives.explanation:
An eval dataset is a claim about what the system will face in production, so its authority comes from its source. The core of a golden set should be drawn from real (anonymized) production or pilot traffic, because real users produce phrasings, typos, ambiguities, and intents that no team imagines. That core is then deliberately augmented: edge cases that are rare but costly, and adversarial cases — injections, jailbreaks, out-of-scope requests — that traffic alone under-samples. Size matters for statistical signal: a 15-case suite passing 100% mostly measures the suite, and coverage should be stratified across intents so whole categories cannot go untested.

Grading methodology must match output type — this is what 'mixed methodologies' means. Deterministic outputs (codes, structured extractions, classifications) get exact-match or code-graded checks: cheap, fast, and objective. Open-ended outputs (summaries, messages, explanations) get an LLM-as-judge constrained by an explicit rubric with concrete criteria and worked examples — and the judge itself must be validated by measuring its agreement against human labels before its scores are trusted, then revalidated periodically for drift. Human review remains the ground truth, reserved for high-stakes samples and judge calibration because it does not scale to every run.

Two hygiene rules protect the framework's validity over time. First, keep a held-out set that is never used during prompt iteration: any eval you optimize against stops measuring generalization, and a team that tunes every change against the full golden set will watch offline scores climb while production quality falls. Second, treat the dataset as a living artifact: as features ship and the user mix shifts, a frozen golden set drifts away from the served distribution and its pass rate decays into false reassurance — refresh it from current traffic on a cadence and re-baseline.
objectives.whyItMatters: The eval framework is the instrument every other decision reads from. If the dataset misrepresents production traffic, the judge is uncalibrated, or the team has overfit to its own test, then every A/B result, every optimization claim, and every 'ready to ship' call is built on a broken instrument — and the failure surfaces where it is most expensive, in front of users.

examples.title: A two-track grading design for a healthcare product
examples.body: A health-tech firm uses Claude for ICD-10 code extraction and for drafting patient follow-up messages. The architect resists pressure to pick one grading method for both. Codes have single verifiable answers, so they get exact-match checks against labeled encounters — deterministic, cheap, zero judge noise. Messages have many acceptable forms, so they get an LLM judge with a rubric covering accuracy, tone, and reading level, with worked examples of good and bad messages; before trusting it, the team measures the judge's agreement with clinician labels on 200 samples and recalibrates the rubric until agreement is acceptable. Clinicians then review only a small high-stakes sample per release. Each output type gets the strongest grading it admits, and the framework stays fast enough to run on every change.

examples.title: Diagnosing an eval that passes while production fails
examples.body: A fintech budgeting assistant's golden set, built from pilot traffic at launch, still passes at 98% eighteen months later — while support tickets double. The product has since added investment and tax features and shifted toward small-business users, none of which the frozen set contains. The architect refreshes the golden set from recent production traffic, stratified by the new intents, and re-baselines: the true pass rate on the current distribution is far lower, and now visible. The team also institutes a quarterly refresh and a held-out split so the new set cannot quietly rot or be overfit the same way.

pitfalls: Building the golden set entirely from synthetic or PM-written queries — imagined usage inherits the team's blind spots; real traffic is the anchor, synthetic data is the supplement for edge and adversarial coverage.
Trusting an LLM judge without validating it against human labels — the judge is a model too, and an unvalidated judge can be confidently, consistently wrong.
Tuning every prompt change against the full golden set — this overfits the prompt to the test; keep a held-out set that iteration never touches.
Treating a small suite's 100% pass as launch evidence — with 15 cases, a perfect score carries almost no statistical signal and says nothing about uncovered intents.
Freezing the eval set at launch — as features and users shift, dataset drift turns a passing eval into false reassurance; refresh from current traffic on a cadence.

objectives.objective: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
objectives.explanation:
Iterative improvement is a controlled-experiment discipline. The first rule is variable isolation: change one thing at a time — prompt, model version, retrieval depth — and evaluate it independently before combining validated changes. Bundled changes make wins unattributable and regressions undiagnosable, and no amount of statistical power on a confounded experiment can say which change caused what.

The second rule is sequencing: offline before online. Offline evals against the golden set are cheap, fast, and risk-free — they filter out bad candidates before any user sees them. Only variants that pass offline earn online exposure, and that exposure grows with evidence: a canary on a small traffic slice with guardrail metrics (error rate, latency, cost, safety) watched for degradation, then a widening split. For changes where no unvalidated output may reach users at all — clinical tools, regulated advice — shadow deployment runs the variant on real production inputs while logging rather than serving its outputs, buying realistic evidence at zero user-facing risk.

The third rule is statistical honesty. A 2% lift over a day of traffic is usually noise; declare a significance threshold and required sample size before the test, run until they are met, and watch guardrail metrics throughout so a win on the primary metric cannot smuggle in a regression elsewhere. Finally, close the loop with production: triage flagged failures, convert recurring ones into permanent eval cases, and verify fixes against them before release. This feedback-driven loop is what makes quality compound — every user complaint becomes lasting test coverage instead of a ticket that fades.
objectives.whyItMatters: Without experimental discipline, teams ship noise as improvement and cannot retrace their steps when a release regresses. The cost is concrete: confounded releases that take weeks to unwind, rollouts based on underpowered tests that quietly degrade a metric nobody was watching, and feedback signals that accumulate for months without changing system behavior.

examples.title: Sequencing a risky prompt change at a SaaS company
examples.body: A PM wants a rewritten billing-assistant prompt pushed straight to a 50/50 production test. The architect instead runs the sequence: the variant must first beat the current prompt on the offline golden set; passing that, it goes to a 5% canary with guardrail metrics on error rate, latency, and cost, plus automated rollback triggers; only after the canary holds does the split widen to gather significance on the primary metric. The 50/50 answer arrives perhaps a week later than the PM wanted — but a regression would have been caught at 5% exposure instead of in front of half the paying customer base.

examples.title: Untangling a confounded release
examples.body: A retailer bundles a prompt change, a model upgrade, and deeper retrieval into one release; metrics improve, so the pattern repeats — until a bundle regresses sharply and nobody can say why. The architect institutes single-variable iteration: each candidate change is evaluated alone against the golden set, effects are recorded per change, and only validated changes are combined, with a final confirmation run on the bundle. The next regression takes minutes to attribute — the eval history shows exactly which change moved which metric — instead of a two-week archaeology project.

pitfalls: Changing several variables in one release — improvements become unattributable and regressions undiagnosable; a longer test on a confounded bundle just measures the confound more precisely.
Testing in production what could have been filtered offline — offline evals are the cheap safety gate; skipping them spends user trust to learn what a golden set would have shown for free.
Calling an A/B test early because the early delta looks good — small samples produce large random swings; pre-define significance and sample size, and let the test run.
Watching only the primary metric during rollout — a win on task success can hide a loss on latency, cost, or safety; guardrail metrics exist to catch the trade you didn't mean to make.
Collecting user feedback without a loop — thumbs-down data that never becomes eval cases is telemetry, not iteration; recurring failures should turn into permanent regression tests.

objectives.objective: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
objectives.explanation:
LLM system failures cluster into distinguishable categories, and the fix depends entirely on the diagnosis. Prompt failure means the instructions themselves are unclear, conflicting, or accreted into contradiction — the signature is inconsistent behavior that no model tier fixes, such as a prompt that says both 'be extremely concise' and 'explain in full detail'. Hallucination means ungrounded generation — the model states things its context does not support — and in retrieval-augmented systems it is usually a grounding gap: traces show retrieval returned nothing relevant, and the model filled the void fluently. Model mismatch means the task exceeds the tier's capability — the signature is a plateau below target after competent prompt iteration (few-shot, chain-of-thought, decomposition) while a stronger model passes the same eval. Context problems are their own category: instructions honored in short sessions but ignored as context grows point to truncation or lost-in-the-middle effects, a placement problem rather than a wording problem.

The diagnostic method matters as much as the taxonomy. Reproduce the failure first so it can be studied; inspect end-to-end traces to localize which step — retrieval, context assembly, tool call, generation — actually broke; then change one variable at a time and verify against the reproduced cases. Teams that skip this and start swapping prompts, models, and parameters simultaneously generate noise, not knowledge, and typically leave the root cause standing.

Map symptom to fix through the cause. Fabricated citations with empty retrieval results call for fixing the retrieval pipeline and constraining generation to provided sources with an abstention path — not for a 'do not hallucinate' instruction, which cannot supply the missing document. Contradictory format output calls for consolidating the prompt under a single owner — not for a validator-retry loop that institutionalizes the coin-flip as permanent runtime cost. A capability plateau calls for routing hard cases to a stronger tier — not a seventh week of rewording.
objectives.whyItMatters: Misdiagnosis is the most expensive failure mode in LLM operations: teams spend weeks prompt-engineering around a capability ceiling, pay for model upgrades to fix retrieval bugs, and bolt retry loops over contradictions that one prompt edit would resolve. Correct diagnosis converts an open-ended debugging slog into a targeted fix, and trace-based method is what makes diagnosis correct.

examples.title: Tracing a hallucination to its real cause
examples.body: A fintech compliance assistant cites policy clause numbers that do not exist. The tempting fix is a sternly worded 'never fabricate citations' instruction. The architect instead pulls traces for the failing queries and finds that retrieval returned no relevant document on every one — the model was answering from a void. The fix lands in two places: repair retrieval (indexing and query coverage for the missed policies) so grounding arrives, and constrain generation to answer only from provided sources with an explicit 'I cannot find that policy' abstention path. The instruction-only fix would have left the empty-context condition — the actual cause — fully intact.

examples.title: Recognizing a capability ceiling
examples.body: A healthcare team runs multi-step prior-authorization logic on a fast, low-cost tier. Six weeks of skilled iteration — few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, task decomposition — leaves accuracy plateaued far below target, while the top-tier model passes the same eval comfortably. That combination is the diagnostic signature of model mismatch: prompt space has been searched competently and the ceiling did not move, but capability did. The architect stops prompting and reframes the question as economics — route these cases to the stronger tier, or route only low-confidence ones — because no wording will buy reasoning the tier does not have.

pitfalls: Adding 'do not hallucinate' instructions to fix grounding gaps — the model still lacks the source material; fix retrieval and give generation an abstention path instead.
Changing several components at once while debugging — simultaneous prompt, model, and parameter changes destroy attribution; reproduce, read traces, then isolate one variable.
Prompt-engineering indefinitely against a capability ceiling — when strong prompting plateaus and a bigger model passes the same eval, the task is above the tier; route up.
Treating temperature 0 as a groundedness fix — determinism makes the model fabricate the same answer every time, not a grounded one; randomness and grounding are different axes.

Blaming wording for length-dependent failures — instructions that work in short sessions but fail at 150K tokens indicate lost-in-the-middle context problems; fix placement and compaction, not phrasing.

objectives.objective: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
objectives.explanation:
Optimization begins with measurement, not levers. Before changing anything, instrument the pipeline to attribute latency and cost across stages — retrieval, queueing, tool calls, generation — because each answer implies a different fix and intuition about the bottleneck is routinely wrong. The goal is movement toward the cost-performance frontier: for a given quality bar, the cheapest and fastest configuration that clears it.

The levers rank roughly by risk to behavior. Prompt caching is usually first: a large stable prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, reference material) resent on every call can be cached so repeat calls pay a small fraction of the input rate, cutting cost and latency with zero effect on outputs. Context trimming — removing redundant instructions, stale history, unused tool schemas — reduces the variable term. Output-length control matters doubly, because output tokens cost more and generation time scales with them: shorter outputs are cheaper and faster. Streaming does not reduce total latency but transforms perceived latency, turning a long blank wait into sub-second time-to-first-token — decisive for interactive users, irrelevant for pipelines. Structural levers come next: routing sends easy cases (often the large majority) to a smaller, cheaper model with escalation of complex or low-confidence cases to the top tier, matching spend to task difficulty. Batch processing prices asynchronous workloads at roughly half the synchronous rate — the right modality for any job where nobody waits on individual responses.

Every lever with behavioral risk — tier changes, aggressive trimming, routing thresholds — must be validated against the eval suite before rollout, and cost comparisons must stay honest by using cost per successful outcome rather than per token. A cheaper configuration that fails more often, retries more, or needs more human correction can be the expensive one.
objectives.whyItMatters: Token spend and latency are where LLM systems most visibly succeed or fail as businesses: a system that clears every quality bar but costs triple budget or feels frozen to users does not survive. The frontier mindset — measured bottlenecks, risk-ranked levers, eval-gated changes — is what lets teams cut cost severalfold without the silent quality regressions that give optimization a bad name.

examples.title: Stacking levers on an overspending assistant
examples.body: A retail assistant answers everything with the top-tier model at triple budget, resending a 30K-token stable prefix each call, while 80% of traffic is simple FAQs the smallest model handles perfectly in offline tests. The architect sequences the levers by risk: prompt caching on the stable prefix first (no behavior change, immediate savings on the dominant cost term), then a router that classifies queries and sends simple ones to the small model with escalation on complexity or low confidence — hard-case quality preserved by design, validated against the golden set before rollout. The two levers compound, and neither required touching the quality bar.

examples.title: Fixing perceived latency without a model change
examples.body: Telehealth clinicians report the summary assistant 'hangs': nothing for 12 seconds, then a wall of text. Traces show retrieval takes under a second — generation dominates, inflated by boilerplate clinicians skip. Instead of a faster tier (quality risk) or more capacity (standing cost), the architect streams tokens so text appears in under a second, and constrains output to the sections clinicians actually use, cutting real generation time and token spend at once. Perceived and actual latency both improve, with no trade on content anyone reads — the levers matched to what the trace evidence showed.

pitfalls: Optimizing before profiling — picking the lever by intuition or implementation ease routinely targets a stage contributing a fraction of the latency or cost; the bottleneck is an empirical fact.

Downgrading model tier as the first cost move — caching, trimming, and output control usually deliver large savings with zero quality risk; spend behavioral risk only after risk-free levers are exhausted.
Judging savings per token instead of per successful task — a cheaper model that triggers retries and human correction can raise true cost while the token dashboard shows improvement.

Applying streaming to non-interactive pipelines — streaming changes perceived latency for a human watching; batch jobs and queues gain nothing from it, while batch pricing is the lever they actually qualify for.
Shipping optimization changes without eval gating — trimming, routing, and tier changes alter behavior; every such change needs a golden-set pass before it earns production traffic.

objectives.objective: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
objectives.explanation:
Production observability for LLM systems rests on content-level structured logging: prompts, completions, and tool calls — not just status codes — correlated by request ID, with PII redaction and retention policies to reconcile debuggability with privacy obligations. An LLM's failure lives in what was said, so logs that record only that a request occurred cannot reconstruct why it went wrong. For multi-step agents the unit of observability is the step: every model call and tool invocation traced with its inputs and outputs under one trace ID, so investigators can walk the chain and find where a run diverged instead of guessing from the final output.

On top of logging sit dashboards and alerts for operational metrics — token usage, cost, latency percentiles, error rates. Alerting should fire on sustained rate thresholds tied to SLOs, not on individual failures: per-event paging produces alert fatigue, and a page nobody reads protects nothing. But operational metrics share a blind spot — they cannot see answer quality. A system can stay green on cost, latency, and errors for weeks while its answers quietly degrade. Quality monitoring therefore needs its own layer: automated scoring of sampled production outputs (an LLM judge against the eval rubric) for coverage, paired with sampled human review on a regular cadence for ground truth and judge calibration.
objectives.whyItMatters: Monitoring is how a system that passed evaluation stays trustworthy after launch, when the input distribution, the knowledge base, and user behavior all keep moving. Teams that log only status codes cannot reconstruct incidents for customers or regulators; teams that watch only operational dashboards learn about quality regressions from enterprise escalations; teams without drift detection discover annually what they could have known in days.

examples.title: Making a multi-step agent debuggable
examples.body: A hospital group's claims agent chains twelve model calls and tool invocations, and 7% of runs end in wrong determinations — but only final outputs are logged, so every investigation restarts from guesswork. The architect implements per-step tracing: each eligibility lookup, code validation, retrieval, and drafting call logged with its inputs and outputs under a single trace ID. The next investigation is a read, not a reproduction: the trace shows the eligibility tool returning stale data at step three, which every later step faithfully propagated. Failure localization drops from days to minutes, and the stale-data case becomes a permanent eval fixture.

examples.title: Closing the quality blind spot
examples.body: A SaaS knowledge assistant's dashboards — cost, tokens, latency, errors — stayed green for six weeks after a knowledge-base migration while answer quality degraded, until enterprise customers escalated. The architect adds the missing layer: automated quality scoring of sampled production outputs against the eval rubric, drift detection comparing production input and output distributions to the eval baseline, and a weekly rubric-graded human review sample as ground truth. Rerun against the incident, the drift detector would have flagged the post-migration shift within days — the blind spot was structural, not a matter of watching the old dashboards harder.

pitfalls: Logging status codes without content — you cannot debug what you did not record; incident reconstruction requires the prompts, completions, and tool calls themselves, redacted and retention-managed.

Assuming green operational dashboards mean good answers — cost, latency, and error metrics are blind to quality; degradation needs its own monitored signal or customers become the detection mechanism.
Paging on every individual failure — per-event alerts produce fatigue and ignored pages; alert on sustained error-rate or latency breaches tied to SLOs so every page is actionable.
Logging only final outputs of multi-step agents — a wrong determination usually crystallizes upstream; without per-step traces, localization is guesswork across the whole chain.
Relying on periodic manual audits to catch drift — slow degradation accumulates between quarterly reviews; continuous drift detection against the eval baseline surfaces distribution shifts in days.
